title: Book 7 — Polymnia, Chapter 46
paragraphs: His uncle Artabanus — the same man who had at first boldly given his opinion advising Xerxes not to march against Greece — noticing that Xerxes was in tears, asked him: “O king, how different are the things you are doing now from those of a moment ago! Having just declared yourself a happy man, you are now shedding tears.” Xerxes answered: “Yes — for when I reckoned the matter over, pity stole over me at the thought how brief is the whole life of man, seeing that of all these multitudes not one will be alive a hundred years from now.” Artabanus replied: “In the course of our life we are subject to a thing more pitiable still: though life is so short, no one, of these men or of others, is by nature so happy that there will not come upon him many times — not just once — the wish to be dead rather than alive; for misfortunes falling upon us, and diseases disturbing our happiness, make the span of life, short as it is, seem long. Thus, since life is full of trouble, death has become the most welcome refuge for man; and God, having given him a taste of the sweetness of life, is shown in this matter to be full of envy.”
